title: Thinking Doesnt Have to Wait for Knowledge
author: Give Spark
summary: This article by Give Spark challenges the assumption that students must accumulate knowledge before they are allowed to think, arguing that the knowledge demand of any question is a design choice made by the teacher, not a fixed property of the topic. Using chess as the entry point, the author draws on de Groot's 1940s research showing that chess masters did not search further ahead than weaker players but recalled real game positions almost perfectly -- because years of play had given them stored patterns to recognise, not because they had superior thinking machinery. Chase and Simon's extension established that the masters' recall advantage vanished on randomly arranged boards, where learned patterns were useless -- confirming that the masters were working from knowledge, not raw cognitive power. The article then makes its central move: if a question requires expert knowledge before thinking can begin, a teacher can rewrite the question to demand less prior knowledge while preserving the same cognitive operation. Two chess questions illustrate this: one requiring knowledge of the Najdorf variation, one requiring only the concept of a turn-based game -- both asking the student to weigh options and predict outcomes, but with different prices of entry. The article explicitly defends knowledge throughout, distinguishing its argument from a knowledge-vs-thinking binary: knowledge and thinking are partners, and the question is about sequence design, not about which matters more. The practical takeaway is that before asking whether students know enough to answer a question, teachers should ask whether the question can be rewritten to enable genuine reasoning at the student's actual level of knowledge.
points: * The knowledge demand of a question is a design choice: a teacher can preserve the cognitive operation (weighing options, considering trade-offs) while raising or lowering how much prior knowledge students need before they can begin thinking. * De Groot's chess research establishes that expert performance is pattern-recognition on familiar configurations, not superior thinking machinery -- masters fail on random boards just as novices do, because their advantage is stored knowledge, not cognition. * The article defends knowledge against misreading: this is not an argument against knowledge-first teaching but against the assumption that thinking must always wait until knowledge is fully acquired -- knowledge and thinking are partners, not a sequence. * Willingham's principle -- that critical-thinking skills are bound up with knowledge of the thing being thought about -- is used to frame the actual argument: the sequence is what needs questioning, not the importance of knowledge itself. * Practical implication: before setting a question, teachers should ask whether the knowledge demand matches what students actually know, and if not, whether the question can be rewritten to enable the intended thinking without demanding unavailable knowledge.
quotes: For most people, not much. Unless you play chess, there is nowhere for your thinking to go. You cannot reason about the Najdorf because you do not know what the Najdorf is. The problem is not that you are not clever enough. The problem is that you do not have the knowledge the question demands.

Both questions are about the same thing: the value of position and first-move advantage in a turn-based game. The thinking they ask for is almost identical. Weigh the options. Consider the trade-offs. Predict the outcome. What separates them is not the difficulty of the thinking. It is the amount of knowledge you need before you are allowed in.

Every question you ask a child carries a knowledge demand, an amount they must already know before they can begin to think. And that demand is not fixed by the topic. It is set by you, in the wording, whether you notice you are setting it or not.

Shown a real game position for a few seconds, masters could reconstruct it almost perfectly from memory. Weaker players could not. On the random boards, their advantage almost vanished. They were no better than beginners.

The masters did not have better memories. They had more knowledge. Years of play had given them stored patterns, familiar configurations of pieces they recognized at a glance. On a real board, those patterns did the heavy lifting. On a random board, the patterns were useless, and the masters had nothing to fall back on.
None of this means knowledge does not matter. Knowledge and thinking are not opponents. They are partners. The more you know about a topic, the more you can do with it.
This is not a case against knowledge. The case is against a particular sequence: the assumption that knowledge must always come first, and thinking can only come after.
